findings.claim: The ruling has one node `changes` write one file per iteration, `<slug>.changes.<n>.txt`, but the juror and the reviewer of the same iteration n need the branch at two different points: the juror before the mend commit, the reviewer after it.
findings.failure_scenario: In iteration n, `juror` (landing-design.md:110-121) runs before `mend-code`/`mend-tests` and `review` (:160-171) runs after the mend commits. If `changes` depends on `hear`, it writes the file before the mend, and `review` reads a log -p without the commit it must judge, which is the G-98 scenario left standing. If `changes` runs after the mender, the juror has no file for iteration n, and on iteration 1 no file at all. The file name is keyed by n and the design's writes use cp -n semantics, so the file cannot be rewritten between the two readers. The ruling names neither a second write nor where the node sits, so applying it as written fixes the defect for at most one of the two roles.

findings.claim: The ruled text writes the file from a bare `git -C <tree> log -p`, without the range `$onto.output.head..$INPUTS.branch` that G-98's option (b) and both role contracts carry ('the branch past the checkout's HEAD', landing-design.md:413, :449).
findings.failure_scenario: A node built to the ruling dumps the patch of every commit in the repository's history into the changes file. The juror and the reviewer then read it on every iteration of a loop that can run up to 200 times (landing-design.md:99). That spends tokens on history the sequence does not need, a CLAUDE.md 1.3 defect. It also buries the branch's own commits, which are the only ones the roles are asked to judge.
